title: Sanctification and Holiness
summary: God's call and power to make His people holy: the meaning of sanctification, the main views of how it happens, and holy living today.
description: "Follow... holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord" (Hebrews 12:14). This course explains what holiness is, how sanctification relates to salvation, and the different ways Reformed, Wesleyan-Holiness (including Deeper Life), Keswick and Pentecostal Christians understand the work of sanctification. It then turns to the practical means of growth and to holiness in speech, body, money and relationships.
objectives: Explain the biblical meaning of holiness and sanctification
Distinguish positional, progressive and final sanctification
Present fairly the Reformed, Wesleyan-Holiness and Keswick views
Describe the means God uses to sanctify believers
outcomes: Describe the three tenses of sanctification
Compare the main views of sanctification fairly
Explain the believer's struggle with sin from Romans 6-8
Plan practical steps for holy living

modules.title: Be Ye Holy
modules.intro: Holiness begins with God. This week we see what holiness is and why God calls His people to it.

lessons.title: The holiness of God
lessons.body:
Holiness means being set apart: separate from sin and devoted to God. God is holy in the highest sense. The seraphim cry, "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts" (Isaiah 6:3).

Because God is holy, His people must be holy: "as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation; Because it is written, Be ye holy; for I am holy" (1 Peter 1:15-16, quoting Leviticus 11:44).

Holiness is not a strange extra for a few special believers. It is the family likeness of God's children.

lessons.title: Separation and devotion
lessons.body:
Holiness has two sides. **Separation from** sin and the world's ways: "Come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing" (2 Corinthians 6:17). "Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world" (1 John 2:15).

**Devotion to** God: "present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God" (Romans 12:1).

Holiness is not withdrawal from people. Jesus prayed, "I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil" (John 17:15). We are in the world but not of it.

lessons.title: Without which no man shall see the Lord
lessons.body:
Scripture insists on holiness: "Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord" (Hebrews 12:14). "This is the will of God, even your sanctification" (1 Thessalonians 4:3).

This does not mean we earn heaven by holiness; we are saved by grace. It means that grace always produces holiness. "The grace of God that bringeth salvation... teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly" (Titus 2:11-12).

A professed faith that leaves a person unchanged should be examined (2 Corinthians 13:5).

terms.def: Being set apart from sin and devoted to God.
God's work of making His people holy.
Turning away from sin and worldly ways.
Dedicating oneself wholly to God's service.
Loving and following the values of a world in rebellion against God.
Offering one's whole self to God in daily obedience (Romans 12:1).

texts.teaches: The LORD of hosts is holy, holy, holy.
Be ye holy; for I am holy.
Come out from among them and be separate.
Without holiness no man shall see the Lord.
This is the will of God, even your sanctification.

summary: Holiness means being set apart from sin and to God.
God's people must be holy because He is holy.
Holiness is separation from sin, not withdrawal from people.
Grace always produces holiness.

questions.q: What does holiness basically mean?
Why must God's people be holy, according to 1 Peter 1:16?
What did Jesus pray in John 17:15?
options: Keep them from evil, not take them out of the world
Take them out of the world

questions.q: What does Titus 2:11-12 say grace teaches us?
options: To deny ungodliness and live godly

modules.title: Three Tenses of Sanctification
modules.intro: Sanctification is past, present and future. This week we study each tense and the believer's struggle with sin.

lessons.title: Positional: set apart in Christ
lessons.body:
In one sense every believer is already sanctified. Paul writes to the troubled Corinthian church, "to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints" (1 Corinthians 1:2). "Ye are washed, but ye are sanctified" (6:11).

"By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all" (Hebrews 10:10).

This is **positional** or definitive sanctification: at conversion we are set apart as God's own, made "saints", and freed from sin's reign. "Our old man is crucified with him... that henceforth we should not serve sin" (Romans 6:6).

lessons.title: Progressive: growing in grace
lessons.body:
Sanctification is also a process. "We all... are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord" (2 Corinthians 3:18). Peter commands, "grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord" (2 Peter 3:18).

It is a work of God and of the believer together: "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do" (Philippians 2:12-13).

We "put off" the old ways and "put on" the new man (Ephesians 4:22-24).

lessons.title: Final: made perfect at His coming
lessons.body:
Sanctification will be completed when Christ returns. "We know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is" (1 John 3:2). God, who began a good work in us, "will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:6).

Then believers will be presented "faultless before the presence of his glory" (Jude 24), with bodies raised in glory (1 Corinthians 15:42-44).

This hope motivates holiness now: "every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure" (1 John 3:3).

terms.def: Being set apart to God once for all at conversion.
The lifelong process of growing in holiness.
The final completion of sanctification when Christ returns.
Holy ones; the New Testament name for all believers.
The person we were before Christ, crucified with Him (Romans 6:6).
Paul's picture of laying aside sinful ways and taking up Christlike ones.

texts.teaches: Believers are sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be saints.
We are sanctified through Christ's offering once for all.
Believers are changed into Christ's image from glory to glory.
Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.
God will complete the good work He began in us.

summary: Positional: believers are set apart as saints at conversion.
Progressive: we grow in holiness as God works and we obey.
Final: we will be made like Christ at His appearing.
The hope of His coming motivates purity now.

questions.q: What is positional sanctification?
options: Being set apart to God at conversion

questions.q: Which verse speaks of being changed from glory to glory?
When will sanctification be completed?
What does the New Testament call all believers?

modules.title: The Battle with Sin
modules.intro: Believers still struggle with sin. This week we study Romans 6-8 and how the Spirit gives victory.

lessons.title: Dead to sin, alive to God
lessons.body:
Romans 6 answers the question, "Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid" (6:1-2).

Paul gives three steps:

1. **Know** that you died with Christ and rose with Him (6:3-6).
2. **Reckon** yourselves "to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God" (6:11).
3. **Yield** your members as instruments of righteousness (6:13).

"For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace" (6:14). Sin may remain, but it no longer reigns.

lessons.title: The struggle of Romans 7
lessons.body:
In Romans 7 Paul describes a painful struggle: "the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do" (7:19). "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" (7:24).

Christians interpret this passage differently. Many Reformed and Baptist teachers see it as Paul's experience as a mature believer, showing that the struggle continues all through life. Many Wesleyan, Holiness and Pentecostal teachers see it as describing a person under the law, trying in their own strength, before the deliverance of Romans 8.

Both agree on the answer: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord" (7:25).

lessons.title: Victory through the Spirit
lessons.body:
Romans 8 is the chapter of the Spirit: "For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death" (8:2). Those who "walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit" fulfil the righteousness of the law (8:4).

"If ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live" (8:13). Victory is not by willpower alone but by the Spirit's power as we cooperate.

Temptation will come, but "God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape" (1 Corinthians 10:13).

terms.def: To count as true; to consider oneself dead to sin and alive to God (Romans 6:11).
Sin's ruling power, broken for believers (Romans 6:14).
To present oneself and one's body to God for righteous use.
Sin that remains in the believer though it no longer reigns.

terms.term: Law of the Spirit of life
terms.def: The Spirit's power in Christ that frees from the law of sin and death (Romans 8:2).
God's provision in every temptation (1 Corinthians 10:13).

texts.teaches: Reckon yourselves dead to sin but alive to God.
Sin shall not have dominion over you.
Paul cried, 'O wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me?'
The law of the Spirit of life frees from the law of sin and death.
God makes a way to escape every temptation.

summary: Romans 6: know, reckon and yield; sin no longer reigns.
Romans 7 is read either as the mature believer's struggle or as life under the law.
Romans 8: victory comes through walking in the Spirit.
God always provides a way of escape from temptation.

questions.q: What are the three steps of Romans 6?
Which chapter is called the chapter of the Spirit?
How do many Wesleyan teachers read Romans 7?
options: As life under the law before Romans 8 deliverance

questions.q: What does God provide with every temptation?

modules.title: How Does God Sanctify?
modules.intro: Christians agree that God sanctifies, but differ on how. This week we present the main traditions fairly.

lessons.title: The Reformed view: lifelong growth
lessons.body:
Reformed Christians, including many Baptists, teach that sanctification is definitive at conversion and progressive throughout life, but never complete before death or Christ's return.

They stress that "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves" (1 John 1:8), and that even Paul said, "Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect" (Philippians 3:12).

On this view, believers make real progress against sin by the Spirit and the means of grace, but remain in conflict until glory. Holiness is a daily, lifelong pursuit.

lessons.title: The Wesleyan-Holiness view: entire sanctification
lessons.body:
John Wesley taught **Christian perfection**, and the Holiness movement developed this as **entire sanctification**: a definite work of grace after conversion, received by faith, in which the heart is cleansed from inbred sin and filled with perfect love.

Deeper Life Bible Church, founded by W. F. Kumuyi, teaches sanctification as a second definite work of grace, after salvation and before the baptism in the Holy Spirit.

They point to texts such as "the very God of peace sanctify you wholly" (1 Thessalonians 5:23), "Be ye therefore perfect" (Matthew 5:48) and "the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin" (1 John 1:7). They emphasise that this is not sinless perfection in knowledge or judgement, and that growth continues afterwards.

lessons.title: Keswick and Pentecostal views
lessons.body:
The **Keswick** or Higher Life movement, beginning in England in 1875, taught that believers can enter a life of continual victory over known sin by full surrender and trusting Christ moment by moment. The sinful nature is counteracted, not removed.

Many **Pentecostals** stress progressive sanctification and the Spirit's empowering, while Holiness Pentecostals keep a crisis experience of sanctification before Spirit baptism.

All these traditions agree that God commands holiness, that it comes by grace and the Spirit, and that believers must actively pursue it. The differences concern whether a decisive second experience is promised and what it accomplishes.

terms.def: In Wesleyan-Holiness teaching, a definite work of grace after conversion cleansing the heart from inbred sin.
Wesley's term for a heart filled with perfect love to God and others.
A distinct experience after conversion, such as entire sanctification in Holiness teaching.
In Holiness teaching, the sinful nature inherited from Adam, which sanctification cleanses.
A movement teaching victorious Christian living through surrender and faith.
Love for God and neighbour that fills the heart and casts out fear (1 John 4:18).

texts.teaches: The God of peace sanctify you wholly.
Paul had not already attained or been made perfect.
The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin.
I am crucified with Christ; Christ lives in me.
Cleanse yourselves from all filthiness, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.

summary: Reformed: sanctification is definitive and progressive, completed only in glory.
Wesleyan-Holiness (including Deeper Life): entire sanctification as a second definite work of grace.
Keswick: victory through surrender and moment-by-moment faith.
All agree holiness is commanded and comes by grace and the Spirit.

questions.q: Who is associated with Christian perfection?
Deeper Life teaches sanctification as:
options: A second definite work of grace

questions.q: Which movement began in England in 1875?
Which text do Reformed teachers cite against present perfection?

modules.title: Holiness in Everyday Life
modules.intro: Holiness is lived out in ordinary places. This week we study the means of grace and holiness in speech, body, money and relationships.

lessons.title: The means of grace
lessons.body:
God uses ordinary means to make us holy:

- **The Word**: "Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth" (John 17:17).
- **Prayer**: "Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation" (Matthew 26:41).
- **Fellowship**: "exhort one another daily... lest any of you be hardened" (Hebrews 3:13).
- **The Lord's Supper and worship**.
- **Trials**: God disciplines us "that we might be partakers of his holiness" (Hebrews 12:10).

Holiness does not grow by accident. "Exercise thyself rather unto godliness" (1 Timothy 4:7).

lessons.title: Holy speech and holy body
lessons.body:
**Speech**: "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth" (Ephesians 4:29). Lies, gossip, insults and crude jokes have no place in a holy life (Ephesians 5:4; Colossians 3:8-9).

**Body**: "Flee fornication... your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost" (1 Corinthians 6:18-19). Each should "possess his vessel in sanctification and honour" (1 Thessalonians 4:4). Holiness includes what we watch (Psalm 101:3), modesty in dress (1 Timothy 2:9), and avoiding drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18).

Holiness begins in the heart: "Keep thy heart with all diligence" (Proverbs 4:23).

lessons.title: Holy money and holy relationships
lessons.body:
**Money and work**: holiness means honesty in business, no bribery, no exploitation. "Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour" (Ephesians 4:28). "The love of money is the root of all evil" (1 Timothy 6:10).

**Relationships**: holiness shows in forgiving others (Colossians 3:13), faithfulness in marriage (Hebrews 13:4), honouring parents, and refusing tribalism and partiality (James 2:1-4).

True holiness is not harsh or proud. It is Christlike: full of love, joy and humility. "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind" (Colossians 3:12).

terms.def: The ordinary ways God uses to grow His people, such as the Word, prayer and fellowship.
A life shaped by reverence for God and devotion to Him.
The believer's body, where the Spirit dwells (1 Corinthians 6:19).
Unwholesome speech that tears down rather than builds up.
Decency and humility in dress and behaviour.
Favouring some people over others because of status, wealth or tribe.

texts.teaches: Sanctify them through thy truth; thy word is truth.
God disciplines us so we may share His holiness.
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth.
Your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost.
As God's elect, put on mercy, kindness and humility.

summary: God sanctifies through the Word, prayer, fellowship, worship and trials.
Holiness governs our speech and our bodies.
Holiness governs money, work and relationships.
True holiness is loving, humble and Christlike.

questions.q: According to John 17:17, how are believers sanctified?
Why should believers flee fornication?
options: The body is the temple of the Holy Ghost

questions.q: What does James 2 warn against?
What should mark true holiness?

short.q: What are the two sides of holiness?
short.model: Separation from sin and the world's ways, and devotion to God.

short.q: Explain the three tenses of sanctification.
short.model: Positional: set apart at conversion; progressive: growing in holiness; final: made like Christ when He appears.

short.q: What are the three steps in Romans 6?
short.model: Know that we died and rose with Christ, reckon ourselves dead to sin and alive to God, and yield our members to righteousness.

short.q: Summarise the Wesleyan-Holiness view of entire sanctification.
short.model: A definite second work of grace after conversion, received by faith, cleansing the heart from inbred sin and filling it with perfect love.

short.q: Summarise the Reformed view of sanctification.
short.model: Sanctification is definitive at conversion and progressive throughout life, never complete until glory.

short.q: Name three means of grace and explain one.
short.model: The Word, prayer and fellowship; for example, the Word sanctifies us because it is truth (John 17:17).

List four areas of everyday holiness.

assignments.title: Views of sanctification
assignments.prompt: Compare the Reformed and Wesleyan-Holiness views of sanctification. Explain each fairly with its main texts, show where they agree, and explain how a believer from either tradition can pursue holiness wholeheartedly.

assignments.title: A personal holiness plan
assignments.prompt: Choose two areas of everyday holiness from Week 5 where you need to grow. For each, explain the biblical teaching, name the means of grace you will use, and set out practical steps for the next month.
